faq.q: Why does pulmonary edema cause crackles?

faq.a: Severe falciparum malaria can cause capillary leak leading to non‑cardiogenic edema.
It helps confirm diagnosis, but in settings without radiography, clinical assessment guides treatment.

exam: A 45‑year‑old with rheumatic mitral stenosis presents with sudden breathlessness – what immediate step and why? — Give supplemental O₂, assess JVP, start IV diuretic; reduces hydrostatic pressure.
How does you differentiate cardiogenic from non‑cardiogenic edema without BNP? — Use bedside echo, JVP, presence of peripheral oedema, and clinical context.
Why is nitroglycerin useful in hypertensive pulmonary edema but risky in septic shock? — It reduces preload and afterload, improving pulmonary congestion; in septic shock it can worsen hypotension.

A patient with severe malaria develops respiratory distress – what is the pathophysiology and first management? — Capillary leak (permeability edema); give O₂, consider diuretics only if volume overloaded, treat malaria urgently.
What are the red‑flag signs that require transfer to a higher‑level facility? — Refractory hypoxaemia, need for mechanical ventilation, hemodynamic instability.
Explain why a patient with nephrotic syndrome may develop pulmonary edema despite normal heart function. — Low oncotic pressure from hypoalbuminaemia promotes fluid shift into lungs.
When is prone positioning indicated in pulmonary edema? — In severe ARDS when conventional ventilation fails, to improve V/Q matching.
Why might a patient with TB pleuritis present with pulmonary edema? — Tuberculous pericarditis can cause constrictive physiology, raising left‑sided pressures.
ai.title: Pulmonary Edema
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Accumulation of fluid in the lung interstitium and alveoli impairs gas exchange. Recognise causes, severity, and urgent management, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Cardiogenic: left‑sided heart failure, rheumatic valve disease, hypertensive crisis.
Non‑cardiogenic: severe infection (malaria, TB, pneumonia), sepsis, ARDS, high‑altitude, inhalation injury, nephrotic syndrome.
sections.p: Pulmonary edema is excess fluid in the lung interstitium and alveoli, reducing oxygen diffusion and causing dyspnoea. It can be cardiogenic or non‑cardiogenic.

b: Hydrostatic edema: ↑capillary pressure (e.g., LV failure).
Permeability edema: ↑capillary leak (e.g., ARDS, severe malaria).
Severity: mild (dyspnoea on exertion), moderate (resting dyspnoea, crackles), severe (hypoxaemia, pink frothy sputum).
sections.p: Understand the Starling forces, differentiate hydrostatic vs. permeability edema, and use clinical criteria to stage severity.

b: Rapid recognition prevents respiratory arrest.
Identify reversible causes (e.g., treat malaria, manage hypertension).
Prioritise oxygen, diuretics, and treat underlying heart failure.
sections.p: In low‑resource East African hospitals, common precipitants include rheumatic heart disease, severe malaria, TB pleuritis, HIV‑related cardiomyopathy, and herbal nephrotoxicity.

t.b: Is fluid present and what pattern? → Kerley B lines, perihilar ‘bat‑wing’ opacity suggest pulmonary edema; if unavailable, rely on clinical signs.
Oxygen saturation level? → <90% indicates severe hypoxaemia needing supplemental O₂.
Distinguish cardiogenic from non‑cardiogenic? → Elevated supports hydrostatic cause; if unavailable, use bedside echo or JVP assessment.
Left ventricular function and valve disease? → Reduced EF or mitral stenosis confirms cardiogenic source.
Infection screen? → Parasitaemia or leukocytosis guides antimicrobial therapy.

b: Oxygen therapy via nasal cannula or face mask; aim SpO₂ > 92%.
Loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) for hydrostatic edema; avoid if hypovolaemic.
Vasodilators (e.g., nitroglycerin) in hypertensive pulmonary edema; monitor blood pressure.
Treat infections: antimalarials, antibiotics for pneumonia, anti‑TB drugs.
If ARDS, use low‑tidal‑volume ventilation; consider prone positioning if ICU available.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care and monitor response.

b: Pneumonia – fever, focal crackles, consolidation.
Pulmonary hemorrhage – hemoptysis, normal cardiac exam.
Pleural effusion – dullness to percussion, fluid shift on lateral decubitus.

b: BNP may be low in severe sepsis despite pulmonary edema.
Chest X‑ray can be normal in early interstitial edema.
sections.p: Certain tests may be normal early or in specific contexts.

b: Identify pink frothy sputum as a sign of severe hydrostatic edema.
Use the ‘3‑step’ approach: history, exam, targeted investigations.
